Empirical Research Plan: Scarcity, Cognition, and Economic Behaviour in Agricultural Households

────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen method: Difference-in-Differences (panel with household fixed effects, supplemented by an event–study specification).

Rationale
• Resource scarcity follows a predictable agricultural calendar: households move from a “post-harvest plenty” phase to a “lean-season scarcity” phase every year.  
• Each household is observed in both states across multiple years ⇒ we can difference within household (first difference) and across time (second difference).  
• Household FE control for time-invariant heterogeneity; calendar-time*district FE purge common macro and spatial shocks.  
• An event-study (months relative to harvest) allows us to diagnose pre-trends and trace dynamic effects.

Why not IV/RDD?
• The central question is the effect of scarcity itself, not of a potentially endogenous proxy (e.g., income).  
• The quasi-experimental variation created by the agricultural cycle is plausibly exogenous once we net out common seasonal shocks.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
────────────────────────────────────────
Unit of observation  : household-year-month

Treatment variable  : Scarcity_{hym} = 1 if month m is in the lean period (defined as −3, −2, −1 months relative to household h’s main harvest in year y); 0 if month is +1, +2, +3 (baseline “plenty” period).  
• Harvest month for household h in year y is taken from the crop-calendar module or imputed from reported harvest dates.

Control group    : The same households observed in the “plenty” period serve as the counterfactual. Households located in districts whose major crop calendars differ slightly provide additional cross-sectional variation.

Treatment timing   : Recurs every year; we code event-time τ ∈ {−5,…,+5} where τ=0 is harvest. Event-study coefficients β_τ identify the effect relative to τ=+1.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel Trends / No Time-varying Confounders  
 In the absence of scarcity, cognitive and economic outcomes would evolve similarly across months.  
 Plausibility: Agriculture-driven income is the main seasonal shock; we net out month×district FE and control for rainfall to mitigate other seasonality.

A2. No Anticipatory Behaviour that Directly Affects Outcomes Pre-Treatment  
 Households might start changing behaviour before scarcity fully bites. Event-study pre-coefficients test this.

A3. Stable Composition (no selective attrition)  
 Plausibility: The survey tracks the same households annually. We will document attrition and re-weight if necessary.

A4. SUTVA  
 One household entering scarcity does not affect another’s cognition. Reasonable given limited interaction across villages.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. MAIN THREATS & MITIGATION
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Other Seasonal Factors (school holidays, festivals, health shocks)  
 • Include month×district FE.  
 • Control for malaria incidence, festival dummies where possible.  
 • Robustness: drop known festival months.

T2. Anticipation or Buffer-Stock Behaviour  
 • Use narrower definition of “treated” (e.g., last month pre-harvest).  
 • Event-study will reveal whether outcomes change before τ = −3.

T3. Measurement Error in Harvest Dates  
 • Cross-check self-reported dates with satellite vegetation indices (NDVI peaks) and district-level crop calendars.  
 • Robustness: re-estimate using district-level harvest timing instead of household-specific dates.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE
library(lubridate)    # date manipulation
library(did)          # event-study utilities (optional)

# ---- 1. Load and Merge Data ----
hh <- fread("household_panel.csv")          # main survey
calendar <- fread("crop_calendar.csv")      # harvest dates by household
rain <- fread("district_rainfall_monthly.csv")  # control

dt <- merge(hh, calendar, by = c("hh_id","year"))
dt <- merge(dt, rain, by = c("district","year","month"))

# ---- 2. Construct Key Variables ----
# Month difference to harvest
dt[, rel_month := interval(ymd(paste(year, month, "15", sep="-")),
                           ymd(paste(year, harvest_month, harvest_day, sep="-"))) %/% months(1)]

# Treatment indicator: lean season = -3:-1 months
dt[, scarcity := fifelse(rel_month %in% -3:-1, 1L,
                         fifelse(rel_month %in% 1:3, 0L, NA_integer_))]

# Keep only testable periods
dt <- dt[!is.na(scarcity)]

# Outcome examples
dt[, cognition_z := scale(cog_score)]      # standardise
dt[, log_consumption := log(real_consumption)]

# ---- 3. Main DID Regression ----
# Household & month×district FE, cluster by hh_id
did_fit <- feols(cognition_z ~ scarcity | hh_id + factor(month)*district, 
                 cluster = ~hh_id, data = dt)
summary(did_fit)

# ---- 4. Event Study ----
dt[, rel_bin := pmax(pmin(rel_month, 5), -5)]   # cap extremes
es_fit <- feols(cognition_z ~ i(rel_bin, ref = 1) | hh_id + factor(month)*district, 
                cluster = ~hh_id, data = dt)
iplot(es_fit)           # pre-trend visual

# ---- 5. Robustness: Drop Festival Months ----
fest <- c(12,1)   # assume harvest is not in Dec/Jan
robust_dt <- dt[!month %in% fest]
robust_fit <- feols(cognition_z ~ scarcity | hh_id + factor(month)*district, 
                    cluster = ~hh_id, data = robust_dt)
etable(did_fit, robust_fit)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (Scarcity Mindset; Mullainathan & Shafir 2013) predicts cognitive load rises under scarcity, lowering measured cognitive performance and increasing short-term, myopic economic choices.

Prior sign: Scarcity is expected to reduce cognition_z by ~0.10–0.20 standard deviations and raise discount-rate proxies by 5–10 p.p.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Common Trends (parallel pre-trends) ….. 1  
C2. No simultaneous shocks/confounders …… 0.5  
C3. Accurate timing of treatment ………… 0.5  
C4. Stable composition / no attrition …… 1  
C5. Correct functional form / inference … 1  

Overall: 4/5 – credible but contingent on robustness checks for timing and concurrent seasonal shocks.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of plan
